newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: U.S., Japan, S.Korea expect North to avert famine.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Japan, S.Korea expect North to avert famine.

text.p: The United States and South Korea on Monday ruled out large-scale food aid to North Korea until it joined peace talks, despite U.N. warnings that Pyongyang could face famine soon, a South Korean spokesman said.
"We reaffirmed our position that any major assistance could be discussed during four-party peace talks," foreign ministry spokesman Lee Kyu-hyung said.
Lee said U.S., Japanese and South Korean officials met in Seoul to coordinate policies on North Korea and agreed that foreign aid would help Pyongyang to overcome its food shortage.
The four-nation peace talks, involving the two Koreas, the United States and China, are designed to secure a peace treaty to replace an armistice that ended the 1950-53 Korean War.
"North Korea certainly faces difficulties but it could avert famine with one million tonnes of international food supplies," he told Reuters.
Lee said China was due to provide about 500,000 tonnes of grain to North Korea while international aid groups were expected to supply 520,000-530,000 tonnes of food.
The Seoul meeting between the United States and its East Asian allies took place after U.N. officials warned last week that Pyongyang would probably be left with no food by June 20.
The meeting was led by Charles Kartman, U.S. deputy assistant secretary of state, Yu Myung-hwan, a director-general at the South Korean Foreign Ministry, and his Japanese counterpart, Ryozo Kato.
Lee said the three nations agreed there were "signs of famine" in some parts of North Korea but the problem stemmed largely from poor communications and transport infrastructure.
Last week, a U.N. official said North Korea was teetering on the edge of a major humanitarian crisis and needed outside help within weeks.
Catherine Bertini, director of the U.N. World Food Programme (WFP), said people in North Korea were facing starvation, with isolated deaths from malnutrition already being reported.

Peter McDermott, deputy director of emergency programmes at the United Nations Children's Fund, said Pyongyang would have to stop a paltry daily ration of 100 grammes (3.5 oz) of rice to its citizens on June 20 as food supplies and fuel dry up.

Washington and Seoul say humanitarian assistance would be provided to help stave off a catastrophe but Pyongyang must not be allowed to use participation in the four-way talks as leverage to extract food assistance.
The United States has pledged $25 million and South Korea $16 million in response to the WFP's appeal for 200,000 tonnes of food for North Korea, or about $95 million.
North Korea in April agreed to join the four-nation talks if it was first guaranteed large-scale food aid and an easing of U.S. trade sanctions.
"There have been no breakthroughs in recent weeks but the United States and South Korea remain hopeful North Korea will accept our proposal for four-party peace talks," he said.
"There are signs that North Korea is moving towards accepting the peace proposal," Lee said without giving details.
On Monday, nine South Korean Red Cross officials left for China to oversee the delivery of 11,200 tonnes of corn to North Korea from June 12 and 18.
The corn, to be delivered via China, is the first of 50,000 tonnes of food the South Korean Red Cross pledged to supply to the North by the end of July.
